decks.title: Chemical Coordination and Integration, Part 1: Endocrine glands, pituitary, feedback and thyroid
goals: Locate the endocrine glands and state the hormones of the hypothalamus and pituitary
Explain the negative feedback control of thyroxine secretion
State the functions of thyroxine, calcitonin and parathormone, and of the pineal gland and thymus

slides.heading: Hormones and chemical coordination
slides.body_md: Part 1: the glands, the pituitary and the thyroid.

visual.alt: Endocrine gland releases a hormone into the blood which acts on target cells

slides.narration: Besides nerves, the body uses chemical messengers called hormones. A gland releases a hormone into the blood, the blood carries it everywhere, and only the target cells that have the right receptor respond.

slides.heading: Nervous and endocrine coordination
slides.body_md: A **hormone** is a chemical produced by an endocrine gland, carried in the blood, and acting in small amounts on target cells.

visual.alt: Table comparing nervous and endocrine coordination

slides.narration: The two systems work together. Nerves give fast, short responses to specific cells, while hormones give slower and longer lasting effects on any cell that carries the receptor.

slides.heading: The endocrine glands of the human body
slides.body_md: The hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid, **4 parathyroids**, thymus, adrenal glands, pancreas and gonads (ovaries and testes) are the main endocrine organs.

slides.narration: The pituitary is called the master gland, but the hypothalamus controls it. Releasing hormones travel through a small set of blood vessels to the front lobe, whereas two hormones made in the hypothalamus travel along nerve fibres to the back lobe.

slides.heading: Hormones of the pituitary
slides.body_md: The anterior pituitary makes six hormones; the posterior pituitary stores and releases two.

rows: Makes the adrenal cortex secrete glucocorticoids
Contraction of the uterus; milk ejection

visual.alt: Table of pituitary hormones, source and action

slides.narration: Growth hormone and prolactin act directly on tissues. Thyroid-stimulating hormone, ACTH, and the two gonad-stimulating hormones are called tropic hormones because they control other glands. Oxytocin and ADH come from the back lobe.

slides.body_md: Hypothalamus releases **TRH**, anterior pituitary releases **TSH**, thyroid releases **thyroxine**. Thyroxine in the blood **inhibits** the hypothalamus and pituitary, so the secretion is kept near a set point: **negative feedback**.

slides.narration: When thyroxine is high, it switches off the signals that stimulate the thyroid, so secretion falls. When thyroxine is low, the brake is released and secretion rises. This keeps the level steady.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a feedback loop in numbers
slides.body_md: After part of the thyroid is removed, thyroxine is 40 percent of normal. In a model, TSH is 100 plus the shortfall of thyroxine, and each step thyroxine gains one quarter of the gap between TSH and thyroxine. Find TSH and the next two values of thyroxine.

visual.alt: Worked table of thyroxine and TSH over the first four steps

slides.narration: A low thyroxine level makes the pituitary release much more of the thyroid-stimulating hormone. The thyroid then produces more thyroxine, so it climbs toward normal while the stimulating hormone falls back. This is how negative feedback corrects a deficit.

slides.heading: The feedback loop over time
slides.body_md: Thyroxine returns step by step to the set point and TSH falls back to its normal level: the loop **corrects itself**.

slides.heading: Thyroid gland
slides.body_md: The **thyroid** makes **thyroxine** (tetraiodothyronine) and **triiodothyronine**, which need **iodine**, and **calcitonin** from its own separate cells.

rows: Raise the basal metabolic rate; help normal growth, brain development and red blood cell formation
Lowers blood calcium by moving calcium into the bones

visual.alt: Table of thyroid hormones and actions

slides.narration: Thyroid hormones set the pace of metabolism and are essential for normal growth and development of the brain. Calcitonin does a different job: it lowers the calcium level in the blood.

slides.heading: Parathyroid, pineal and thymus
slides.body_md: The **4 parathyroid glands** make **parathormone (PTH)**, which **raises** blood calcium; with calcitonin it keeps calcium steady. The **pineal gland** makes **melatonin**; the **thymus** makes **thymosin**.

rows: Raises blood calcium: bone breakdown, kidney reabsorption, gut absorption
Sleep-wake rhythm, body temperature, skin colour, menstrual cycle
Develops T lymphocytes; immunity; shrinks with age

visual.alt: Table of parathyroid, pineal and thymus hormones

slides.narration: Parathormone and calcitonin work in opposite directions, so together they hold blood calcium steady. Melatonin sets the daily rhythm of sleep. Thymosin helps the immune cells mature, and the thymus shrinks in old age.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: calcium below the normal range
slides.body_md: The normal range of blood calcium is taken as 9 to 11 mg per dL. After neck surgery a patient has 7.6 mg per dL. By how much, and by what percent of the lower limit, is she below normal, and which hormone is lacking?
bullets: Shortfall $= 9 - 7.6 = 1.4$ mg per dL.
Percent of lower limit $= \dfrac{1.4}{9} \times 100 = 15.6$ percent.
Low calcium points to too little parathormone, as the parathyroids may have been damaged.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Hormones: chemical messengers in the blood acting on target cells.
Hypothalamus: releasing and inhibiting hormones to the anterior pituitary; oxytocin and ADH stored in the posterior pituitary.
Tropic hormones (TSH, ACTH, LH, FSH) control other glands; thyroxine exerts negative feedback on TRH and TSH.
Thyroid: thyroxine, triiodothyronine, calcitonin. Parathyroid: parathormone raises calcium.
Pineal: melatonin. Thymus: thymosin.

visual.alt: Summary table of glands and hormones

slides.narration: To recap: the hypothalamus controls the pituitary, and the pituitary controls other glands. Thyroxine feeds back to switch itself down, and parathormone and calcitonin balance calcium. Melatonin and thymosin come from the pineal and thymus.

slides.heading: Disorders of growth, thyroid and adrenal glands
slides.body_md: Too little (hypo-) or too much (hyper-) of a hormone causes disease.

rows: Pituitary: too little growth hormone in childhood
Pituitary: too much growth hormone in adults
Coarse face, large hands and feet
Thyroid: too little thyroxine in infancy
Thyroid: lack of iodine, so enlarged gland
Adrenal cortex: too little cortical hormones

slides.narration: In dwarfism the pituitary makes too little growth hormone, and in acromegaly too much. Too little thyroxine in infancy causes cretinism. Lack of iodine causes simple goitre. Too much thyroxine causes exophthalmic goitre. Too little cortical hormone causes Addison disease.

slides.heading: Diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus
slides.body_md: Both cause a large volume of urine, but for different reasons.

rows: Very large volume, dilute, no sugar

visual.alt: Table distinguishing diabetes mellitus from diabetes insipidus

slides.narration: In diabetes mellitus the pancreas makes too little insulin, so blood glucose is high and glucose spills into the urine. In diabetes insipidus the pituitary lacks the antidiuretic hormone, so the kidney cannot save water, but blood glucose is normal.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: water lost in diabetes insipidus
slides.body_md: A healthy adult passes about 1.5 L of urine a day; a patient with diabetes insipidus passes 12 L. Find how many times more urine this is, the extra volume per day and the volume in a week.
bullets: Ratio $= \dfrac{12}{1.5} = 8$ times.
Extra $= 12 - 1.5 = 10.5$ L per day.
Week $= 7 \times 12 = 84$ L.

visual.alt: Worked table: 8 times the normal urine volume

slides.narration: Divide the patient volume by the normal volume, subtract for the extra water lost each day, and multiply by seven for the week. Such a loss explains the intense thirst, since the lost water must be replaced.

sections.heading: 1. The endocrine system, the hypothalamus and pituitary, and feedback
sections.body_md:
A **hormone** is a **chemical messenger** made by an **endocrine (ductless) gland**, carried in the **blood** and acting in very small amounts on **target cells** that have the right **receptor**. Nervous coordination is fast and short; endocrine coordination is slower and longer lasting.

**Endocrine glands of the human body:** hypothalamus, pituitary, pineal, thyroid, **4 parathyroids** (on the back of the thyroid), thymus, adrenals (above the kidneys), pancreas (islets of Langerhans), and the gonads (testes and ovaries). The gut also makes hormones.

**Hypothalamus:** controls the pituitary. It makes **releasing hormones** (for example TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH) and **inhibiting hormones** (for example somatostatin), which reach the **anterior pituitary** through the **hypophysial portal vessels**. It also makes **oxytocin** and **vasopressin (ADH)**, which pass down nerve fibres and are stored and released from the **posterior pituitary**.

**Pituitary (hypophysis)**
| Lobe | Hormone | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Anterior | **Growth hormone (GH)** | Growth of tissues and bones; protein synthesis |
| Anterior | **Prolactin (PRL)** | Growth of the mammary glands; milk formation |
| Anterior | **TSH** (tropic) | Stimulates the thyroid to release thyroxine |
| Anterior | **ACTH** (tropic) | Stimulates the adrenal cortex to release glucocorticoids |
| Anterior | **LH and FSH** (tropic, gonadotropins) | Gonads: gametes and sex hormones |
| Intermediate (small in humans) | **MSH** | Pigment cells of the skin |
| Posterior | **Oxytocin** | Contraction of the uterus at birth; milk ejection |
| Posterior | **ADH (vasopressin)** | Reabsorption of water in the kidney tubules |

**Feedback control of tropic hormones:** a hormone of the target gland usually **inhibits** the hypothalamus and pituitary: **negative feedback**. Thyroxine: hypothalamus (**TRH**) → anterior pituitary (**TSH**) → thyroid (**thyroxine**); thyroxine in the blood **reduces TRH and TSH**, and when thyroxine falls the inhibition is removed and secretion increases. In a simple model with thyroxine at 40 percent of normal, TSH is 160 percent and thyroxine returns to about 100 percent within 8 steps (illustrative values).

sections.heading: 2. Thyroid, parathyroid, pineal and thymus
sections.body_md:
**Thyroid:** a butterfly-shaped gland on the front of the windpipe, with follicles that make **thyroxine (T4, tetraiodothyronine)** and **triiodothyronine (T3)**, for which **iodine** is needed, and **calcitonin (thyrocalcitonin)** from separate cells.
- **Thyroxine and triiodothyronine:** raise the **basal metabolic rate**; support normal growth, development of the brain, and formation of red blood cells; help to control body temperature.
- **Calcitonin:** **lowers** blood calcium by increasing its deposition in the bones.

**Parathyroids:** 4 small glands on the back of the thyroid. **Parathormone (PTH)** **raises** blood calcium: it increases bone breakdown, reabsorption of calcium by the kidney tubules, and absorption of calcium in the gut (with vitamin D). PTH and calcitonin act in opposite directions to keep calcium within limits (the model range used here is 9 to 11 mg per dL; books vary).

**Pineal gland:** makes **melatonin**, which regulates the **sleep-wake (diurnal) rhythm**, body temperature, skin pigmentation and the menstrual cycle.

**Thymus:** makes **thymosin**, which helps the **differentiation of T lymphocytes** and so cell-mediated immunity; the thymus is large in children and **shrinks with age**, so immunity weakens in old age.

sections.heading: 3. Adrenal glands, pancreas, gonads and the gut
sections.body_md:
**Adrenal glands:** on the kidneys; the **cortex** has **3 layers** and the **medulla** inside.
- **Zona glomerulosa** (outer): **mineralocorticoids** (aldosterone): reabsorption of sodium and loss of potassium and so water and blood pressure.
- **Zona fasciculata** (middle): **glucocorticoids** (cortisol): raise blood glucose (gluconeogenesis), break down proteins and fats, **anti-inflammatory**, reduce immunity.
- **Zona reticularis** (inner): small amounts of **sex corticoids** (androgens).
- **Medulla:** **adrenaline (epinephrine) and noradrenaline**: **emergency hormones** (fight or flight): faster, stronger heartbeat, wider pupils, more alertness, sweating, **breakdown of glycogen, fats and proteins** to raise blood glucose.

**Pancreas (islets of Langerhans):** **alpha cells** make **glucagon** (raises blood glucose: glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis in the liver); **beta cells** make **insulin** (lowers blood glucose: uptake by cells, glycogenesis); **delta cells** make **somatostatin** (inhibits both). The fasting blood glucose is taken as 70 to 110 mg per dL in the chapter (book values differ); a diabetic is suspected with fasting glucose of 126 or two-hour glucose of 200 mg per dL or more in a tolerance test.

**Gonads:** **testis** (Leydig cells): **androgens (testosterone)**: male characters, spermatogenesis; **ovary**: **oestrogen** (female characters, cycle) and **progesterone** (maintains pregnancy).

**Gastrointestinal tract:** **gastrin** (stomach: secretion of HCl and pepsinogen), **secretin** (duodenum: water and bicarbonate from the pancreas), **cholecystokinin-pancreozymin, CCK-PZ** (duodenum: contraction of the gall bladder and pancreatic enzymes), **gastric inhibitory peptide, GIP** (inhibits gastric secretion and movement).

Alpha-cell hormone that raises blood glucose.
Medulla hormone for emergencies.

Gut hormone: gall bladder contraction and pancreatic enzymes.

sections.heading: 4. Mechanism of hormone action
sections.body_md:
A hormone acts only on **target cells** that have its **receptor**.

**Protein, peptide and amino acid hormones (insulin, glucagon, adrenaline, TSH):** **water soluble**, cannot cross the lipid membrane. They bind a **receptor on the cell membrane**, which activates **adenylyl cyclase** through a **G protein**; it converts **ATP to cyclic AMP (cAMP)**, the **second messenger**, which activates **protein kinases and enzymes** and produces the response. (The hormone is the first messenger.) The response is **fast**.

**Steroid hormones (cortisol, testosterone, oestrogen) and thyroid hormones:** **lipid soluble**, they **diffuse through the membrane** and bind an **intracellular receptor** (cytoplasm or nucleus). The **hormone-receptor complex** binds **DNA**, switches **genes** on or off, and changes the synthesis of **mRNA and proteins**. The response is **slower** and longer lasting.

*Note on books:* the thyroid hormones are lipid soluble and act on nuclear receptors like steroids, although they are amino acid derivatives; adrenaline acts through cAMP. Some books use the term "chemical nature" (peptide, steroid, amino acid derivative) as the basis of the two mechanisms.

sections.heading: 5. Disorders of hypo- and hypersecretion
sections.body_md:
| Disorder | Gland, hormone and defect | Main features |
|---|---|---|
| **Dwarfism** | Pituitary: **hyposecretion of growth hormone** in childhood | Short stature with normal proportions |
| **Acromegaly** | Pituitary: **hypersecretion of growth hormone** in adults (in children, gigantism) | Enlarged face, hands and feet |
| **Cretinism** | Thyroid: **hyposecretion of thyroxine** in infancy | Stunted growth, mental retardation, low metabolic rate |
| **Goitre** | Thyroid: usually **iodine deficiency**; the gland enlarges as TSH rises | Swelling of the neck; low thyroxine |
| **Exophthalmic goitre (Graves disease)** | Thyroid: **hypersecretion of thyroxine** (autoimmune) | Enlarged thyroid, protruding eyes, high metabolic rate, weight loss |
| **Addison disease** | Adrenal cortex: **hyposecretion of corticoids** | Weakness, low blood pressure, low sodium |
| **Diabetes mellitus** | Pancreas: **lack of insulin** (or poor response) | High blood glucose, glucose in urine, much urine, thirst, weight loss |
| **Diabetes insipidus** | Posterior pituitary: **lack of ADH** | Very large volume of dilute urine, thirst, dehydration; blood glucose normal |

**Diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus** both give frequent urination, but the first is due to lack of **insulin** with high blood glucose and sugary urine; the second is due to lack of **ADH**, with normal blood glucose and sugar-free urine.

key_terms.definition_md: Secretion of less hormone than normal.
Secretion of more hormone than normal.
Enlargement of the thyroid gland.
Disorder from lack of ADH, with very large volumes of dilute urine.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying the pituitary makes oxytocin and ADH (the hypothalamus makes them; the posterior pituitary stores and releases them).
- Mixing up parathormone (raises calcium) and calcitonin (lowers calcium).
- Mixing up insulin (lowers glucose) and glucagon (raises glucose), or the alpha and beta cells.
- Saying thyroxine stimulates TSH (it inhibits it: negative feedback).
- Writing that steroid hormones act through cyclic AMP (they act on intracellular receptors and genes).
- Confusing diabetes mellitus and diabetes insipidus, or acromegaly with gigantism and dwarfism.
- Writing "goitre is caused by too much iodine" (it is lack of iodine, or an overactive gland in Graves disease).

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark subparts: a gland from its position, a hormone from its action, a tropic hormone, a disorder from a case, a give-a-reason.
- 2–3-mark questions: negative feedback of thyroxine; insulin and glucagon; protein against steroid action; diabetes mellitus against insipidus; gut hormones.
- 5-mark questions in parts: pituitary and its hormones; thyroid and parathyroid with disorders; adrenal and pancreatic hormones; mechanism of hormone action.

questions.solution_md: The pituitary is suspended from the hypothalamus by a stalk — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Which of these pituitary hormones acts chiefly by stimulating the secretion of another endocrine gland?
questions.solution_md: ACTH is a tropic hormone: it stimulates the adrenal cortex — option (d).

questions.stem_md: In an experiment on a rat, the hypophysial portal vessels are cut, but the nerve fibres in the pituitary stalk are left intact. Which secretion will be least affected?

Vasopressin (ADH) released from the posterior pituitary

questions.solution_md: Anterior pituitary hormones depend on the releasing hormones carried by the portal vessels; the posterior pituitary is reached by nerve fibres — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A doctor injects a woman in labour with a hormone that strengthens the contractions of the uterus. The injected hormone is chemically like the one released from the
questions.solution_md: Oxytocin is released from the posterior pituitary — option (a).

questions.stem_md: After a long walk in the sun, a hiker has lost much water by sweating. Which hormone helps to conserve water by making the kidney tubules reabsorb more of it?
questions.solution_md: ADH increases water reabsorption in the kidney tubules — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A mother’s mammary glands grow and begin to make milk after delivery. Which pituitary hormone is mainly responsible for the formation of milk?
questions.solution_md: Prolactin stimulates milk formation, while oxytocin ejects it — option (a).

high thyroxine in the blood inhibits the pituitary, so TSH is not released and the gland is not stimulated

questions.solution_md: Negative feedback: a high thyroxine level suppresses TSH, so the thyroid is not stimulated — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Name two tropic hormones of the anterior pituitary and state the gland each acts upon.

answer.model_answer_md: **TSH** (thyroid-stimulating hormone) acts on the **thyroid gland** and makes it release thyroxine; **ACTH** (adrenocorticotropic hormone) acts on the **adrenal cortex** and makes it release glucocorticoids. (LH and FSH likewise act on the gonads.)

questions.solution_md: TSH and ACTH with target glands.

marking_scheme.step: ACTH acting on the adrenal cortex

questions.stem_md: Where are oxytocin and vasopressin made, and where are they stored and released? State one action of each.

answer.model_answer_md: Both are made by neurosecretory cells of the **hypothalamus** and pass down nerve fibres to be **stored and released from the posterior pituitary**. **Oxytocin** causes **contraction of the uterus** (and milk ejection); **vasopressin (ADH)** increases **reabsorption of water** in the kidney tubules.

questions.solution_md: Made in hypothalamus; released from posterior pituitary; actions.

marking_scheme.step: Made in the hypothalamus, released from the posterior pituitary

questions.stem_md: With the help of a flow diagram in words, explain how the secretion of thyroxine is controlled by negative feedback.

answer.model_answer_md: The **hypothalamus** releases **TRH**, which makes the **anterior pituitary** release **TSH**; TSH stimulates the **thyroid** to release **thyroxine**. A **rise in thyroxine** in the blood **inhibits the hypothalamus and the pituitary**, so TRH and TSH fall and thyroid secretion is reduced. When thyroxine falls, the inhibition is lifted and secretion rises, so the level stays near a set point.

questions.solution_md: TRH, TSH, thyroxine; inhibition.

questions.stem_md: A tumour destroys the whole anterior lobe of a young woman’s pituitary gland. Name three bodily functions that would be affected and the hormone concerned in each.

answer.model_answer_md: **Growth** would be affected, because **growth hormone** is lacking; the **thyroid** would be underactive, because **TSH** is lacking, and so would the **adrenal cortex**, because **ACTH** is lacking. Menstrual cycles and fertility would also fail, because **LH and FSH** are lacking, and she would not make milk, because of the lack of **prolactin**.

questions.solution_md: Three functions with hormones.

marking_scheme.step: Adrenal cortex or gonads with ACTH, LH, FSH

questions.stem_md:
(a) Draw a labelled diagram to show how the hypothalamus is connected to the anterior and posterior lobes of the pituitary. [2]
(b) Name the hormones of the anterior pituitary. [2]
(c) Name the two hormones released from the posterior pituitary. [1]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Diagram:** the **hypothalamus** above, with its **releasing and inhibiting hormones** passing through the **portal vessels** to the **anterior lobe**, and **nerve fibres** running down the **stalk** to the **posterior lobe**; the two lobes are labelled.

(b) The anterior pituitary makes **growth hormone, prolactin, thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH), adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), luteinising hormone (LH) and follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)**.

(c) The posterior pituitary stores and releases **oxytocin** and **vasopressin (ADH)**, which are made in the hypothalamus.

questions.solution_md: Diagram of hypothalamus and pituitary; six hormones; two hormones.

questions.stem_md: Read the passage and answer the questions that follow.
questions.passage_md:
Blood tests on three patients with symptoms of thyroid disease gave the results below. (Low and high are relative to the normal range.)

| Patient | Thyroxine | TSH |
|---|---|---|
| A | Low | High |
| B | High | Low |
| C | Low | Low |

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a)** (b) the thyroid gland itself, which cannot respond to the high TSH

**(b)** (c) the pituitary or hypothalamus is failing to stimulate the thyroid

**(c)** (i) Patient B has a **high thyroxine** level. High thyroxine **inhibits the hypothalamus and the pituitary**, so **TRH and TSH are reduced**, and the low TSH is the normal response of the feedback loop.

**OR** (ii) The **high TSH** continues to **stimulate the thyroid** to grow and to try to make more hormone, but because the gland cannot make enough thyroxine, the **feedback does not switch the TSH off**; the gland therefore **enlarges (goitre)**.

questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Low thyroxine with high TSH means the pituitary is responding normally to the lack of thyroxine, so the thyroid is failing — option (b).

**(b)** With a low thyroxine level the TSH should be high; it is low, so the stimulation from above has failed — option (c).

**(c)** (i) High thyroxine inhibits TSH.

(ii) TSH keeps stimulating.

the thyroid gland itself, which cannot respond to the high TSH
the hypothalamus, which makes too much TRH only

options.text_md: the thyroid gland is failing but the pituitary is normal
the pituitary or hypothalamus is failing to stimulate the thyroid
the feedback loop is working normally

children.solution_md: With a low thyroxine level the TSH should be high; it is low, so the stimulation from above has failed — option (c).

children.stem_md: **Either** (i): Explain, using negative feedback, why patient B has a low TSH level.

answer.model_answer_md: Patient B has a **high thyroxine** level. High thyroxine **inhibits the hypothalamus and the pituitary**, so **TRH and TSH are reduced**, and the low TSH is the normal response of the feedback loop.

marking_scheme.step: High thyroxine inhibits hypothalamus and pituitary

alternatives.stem_md: **Or** (ii): Explain why patient A is likely to develop an enlarged thyroid gland.

answer.model_answer_md: The **high TSH** continues to **stimulate the thyroid** to grow and to try to make more hormone, but because the gland cannot make enough thyroxine, the **feedback does not switch the TSH off**; the gland therefore **enlarges (goitre)**.

marking_scheme.step: No effective feedback, so gland enlarges

questions.stem_md: Blood tests show that patient X has a high thyroxine level and a high TSH level, while patient Y has a high thyroxine level and a low TSH level. Which gland is most likely at fault in each patient? Use the idea of negative feedback to explain the difference.

answer.model_answer_md: In **patient Y** the **thyroid** itself is overactive: the high thyroxine **inhibits the pituitary**, so TSH is **low**, as feedback would predict. In **patient X** the TSH is high **in spite of** the high thyroxine, so the **feedback has failed** and the fault lies **above the thyroid**, probably a **pituitary tumour** that makes TSH without responding to thyroxine, which then drives the thyroid to make too much.

questions.solution_md: Y thyroid; X pituitary, feedback fails.

marking_scheme.step: Patient Y: thyroid overactive, TSH suppressed by feedback
Patient X: TSH high despite high thyroxine, so feedback has failed
Fault in the pituitary for X

questions.stem_md: Name two hormones of the thyroid gland that contain iodine and state two functions of them.

answer.model_answer_md: **Thyroxine** and **triiodothyronine** contain iodine. They **raise the basal metabolic rate** and are needed for **normal growth and the development of the brain**; they also help the formation of red blood cells.

questions.solution_md: Two hormones, two functions.

questions.stem_md: Explain how parathormone and calcitonin together keep the calcium level of the blood steady.

answer.model_answer_md: **Parathormone** from the parathyroids **raises** blood calcium by increasing **bone breakdown**, **reabsorption** by the kidney tubules and **absorption** in the gut. **Calcitonin** from the thyroid **lowers** it by promoting **deposition of calcium in the bones**. Their opposite actions keep the level within limits.

questions.solution_md: Opposite actions.

questions.stem_md: Name the hormone of the pineal gland and the hormone of the thymus, and state two functions of each.

answer.model_answer_md: The **pineal gland** secretes **melatonin**, which regulates the **sleep-wake rhythm** and **body temperature** (and affects skin pigmentation and the menstrual cycle). The **thymus** secretes **thymosin**, which promotes the **differentiation of T lymphocytes** and so the **cell-mediated immune response**; the thymus shrinks with age, so immunity weakens in old age.

questions.solution_md: Melatonin and thymosin with functions.

questions.stem_md: Compare the actions of thyroxine, calcitonin and parathormone.

answer.model_answer_md: **Thyroxine** (from the thyroid) **raises the basal metabolic rate** and supports normal growth and the development of the brain. **Calcitonin** (also from the thyroid) **lowers blood calcium** by promoting its deposition in the bones. **Parathormone** (from the parathyroid glands) **raises blood calcium** by increasing the breakdown of bone, the reabsorption of calcium by the kidney tubules and its absorption from the gut, so it opposes calcitonin.

questions.solution_md: Three hormones with actions.

questions.stem_md: Young rats whose parathyroid glands have been removed develop tremors and spasms of their muscles within days. Explain the cause, and say what injection would relieve the signs.

answer.model_answer_md: Without the **parathyroid glands** there is no **parathormone**, so the **calcium level in the blood falls**. Low calcium makes nerves and muscles **over-excitable**, giving tremors and spasms (tetany). The signs would be relieved by an injection of **parathormone** (or of **calcium**), which restores the calcium level.

questions.solution_md: No parathormone; low calcium; treatment.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Name the two hormones of the thyroid gland that control metabolism and state one function of them. [2]
(b) Explain how parathormone and calcitonin regulate the level of calcium in the blood. [2]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) **Thyroxine** and **triiodothyronine**; they **raise the basal metabolic rate** and are needed for **growth and brain development**.

(b) **Parathormone** raises blood calcium through **bone breakdown**, **kidney reabsorption** and **gut absorption**; **calcitonin** lowers it by promoting **deposition in bones**; the two act oppositely and keep the level within limits.

(c) The thyroid makes too little thyroxine, TSH stays high, and the gland **enlarges (goitre)**.

questions.solution_md: Thyroid hormones; calcium control; goitre.

questions.stem_md: Name the cells that make insulin and the cells that make glucagon, and state how the two hormones act on blood glucose.

questions.stem_md: Compare mineralocorticoids and glucocorticoids with respect to the layer of the cortex that makes them, one example and the main action.

questions.stem_md: Explain how the blood glucose of a healthy person is brought back to normal (i) after a sugary meal and (ii) after a long gap without food.

answer.model_answer_md: (i) After a meal, glucose rises and the **beta cells** release **insulin**; the liver, muscle and fat cells **take up glucose** and the liver stores it as **glycogen**, so the level falls. (ii) After a long fast, the level falls and the **alpha cells** release **glucagon**, which makes the liver **break down glycogen** and form glucose, so the level rises.

questions.solution_md: Insulin after a meal; glucagon after a fast.

answer.model_answer_md: A **second messenger** is a substance made **inside the cell** after a hormone (the first messenger) binds its receptor on the membrane, and it passes the message on within the cell.
